strengths: Novel methodological contribution: First work to model brain disorders through targeted VLM ablation, introducing 'digital twins' for computational neuroscience
Well-grounded in neuroscience: Leverages established VWFA-dyslexia theory and uses principled fMRI localizer paradigms for identifying task-selective units

Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple standardized benchmarks (ROAR, RAVEN, Kempler, lexical decision) adapted from human clinical assessments, with strong control experiments (random ablation, layer-type analysis, multiple architectures)
Human-model correspondence: Selective phonological (not orthographic) deficits match dyslexic patterns, and importantly the model produces this despite lacking auditory input
Rigorous experimental design: Results averaged over 20 seeds, appropriate statistical testing, good ablation specificity controls, sensitivity analyses for hyperparameters
Clear presentation: Excellent figures, well-written, methods clearly described, reproducibility prioritized (code promised, statistical details provided)
weaknesses: Model-biology validation gap: Identified VWF-selective units never compared against fMRI data from human VWFA; no confirmation that MLP selectivity relates to biological word-selective neurons

Incomplete human matching: Model shows 8% phonological deficit but 0% orthographic, while humans show both (~9% and ~6%); explanation for this mismatch is incomplete and raises questions about model fidelity
Circular threshold selection: Uses human-derived 65% ROAR dyslexia threshold to determine model ablation magnitude—applies human standard to model without validation that this is appropriate
Causality overclaimed: Presented as testing 'causal hypotheses' but work is fundamentally correlational; showing what happens upon ablation differs from proving causation in human brain

Limited mechanistic insight: Core finding (ablating word-selective units impairs word recognition) is somewhat tautological; does not explain how deficits arise or provide deep mechanistic understanding
Benchmark design limitations: Only 12 RAVEN items is small; 50+50 ROAR test items limited; Kempler adapted to VQA changes original task structure; some adaptation choices appear arbitrary
Incomplete model generalization: Main analysis on single model (Qwen2-VL); LLaVA-NeXT showed poor RAVEN baseline (below chance); only PixTral fully replicated—generalizability unclear
Developmental disorder limitation: Captures 'end-state consequences' not developmental trajectories; dyslexia fundamentally emerges during literacy acquisition, not modeled here

Perturbation discontinuity: Only full ablation produces selective effects; other scaling factors produce incoherent outputs or no effect, suggesting discontinuous regime that raises interpretability concerns

Missing error pattern validation: Error types (gibberish, contextual over-interpretation, hedging) shown in Tables 1-3 but unclear if they match human dyslexic errors or reflect model-specific degradation

strengths: Novel methodology that creatively adapts neuroscience-inspired functional localization methods to identify and causally manipulate VLM representations
Rigorous experimental design with appropriate controls (VWF-selective vs. random ablations), multiple random seeds (n=20), and proper statistical testing across multiple benchmarks

Comprehensive evaluation using multi-faceted tasks (ROAR, RAVEN, Kempler, phonology/orthography dissociation, font sensitivity) that demonstrate both selective reading deficits and preserved visual reasoning
Strong empirical results showing 32% normalized performance drop on reading tasks while preserving general visual intelligence, with generalization across three different VLM architectures
Neural validation through fMRI alignment analysis demonstrating that identified VWF-selective units correspond to human VWFA activity patterns
Practical applications demonstrated through font sensitivity predictions that align with dyslexia-friendly design principles and human user experience
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, detailed methodology, and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Opens a generalizable computational framework potentially applicable to investigating other brain disorders beyond dyslexia
weaknesses: Conceptual gap inadequately addressed: the analogy between ablating VLM units and VWFA hypoactivation, while suggestive, lacks strong biological justification given fundamental differences in computational mechanisms between VLMs and biological brains

Unexplained finding that phonological deficits emerge from visual disruption despite the model never processing auditory input or phonology developmentally, raising questions about whether this mechanism parallels human dyslexia

Circularities in experimental design: dyslexia threshold (65% ROAR) is based on human population statistics without demonstrating equivalent difficulty across modalities; no sensitivity analysis of threshold dependence
Incomplete comparison with human data: orthographic processing discrepancy (Figure 6c) explained speculatively; only one human dataset (Luke et al., 2023) used for phonology/orthography dissociation
Limited evaluation scope: only 100 test items for ROAR, only 3 large-scale models tested (unclear generalization), and English-only tasks despite dyslexia's cross-linguistic relevance

fMRI alignment effects diminish substantially above 1.25% subset size due to feature correlation, and effect sizes at small percentages are non-trivial but modest, raising questions about the strength of neural correspondence
Key finding under-explored: why do only MLP gate projection layers show reading-selective deficits? Why not attention layers? Mechanistic understanding lacking

Overstated framing: paper claims to 'model dyslexia' and 'establish a framework for investigating brain disorders' but really models one hypothesized mechanism (VWFA hypoactivation) while abstracting away genetic, developmental, and etiological factors
Font validation preliminary: only 12 fonts tested against expert recommendations; no validation against actual dyslexic users to confirm ecological validity
Multiple comparisons across many tests without formal correction, and the Kempler task improvement with ablation (p < 0.01) is interesting but underexplored mechanistically
